searchText: **dannyryan** Yeah, if you were visualizing, you might bold the epochs that were directly finalized becuase it is interesting in its own right. If you saw a bunch of epochs that werent bolded and then one that was, might mean the chain had trouble for a bit, but from the perspective of finality, they are all finalized understood thanks for this it helps I was updating our epoch metrics and i guess I need to re-think some of it. so for `beacon_previous_justified_epoch` would that be the one that was finalized via validators, or finalized implicitly? That one would be justified via validators Meaning implicitly will not change that number understood! cool that makes things easy <@322222239850168331> A followup -- Casper is designed in such a way that favors liveness. Disagreeing on the current epoch does not prevent the chain from continuing to be built and to find consensus at a subsequent epoch. The "Plausible Liveness" claim in the FFG paper shows that the chain can finalize future epochs (without requiring slashing honest actors) regardless of any votes previously cast. Ok, I am going to repeat the request for teams to not pull in the ETH 2.0 spec tests every single CI run through LFS. It slows down your clones, consumes a lot of bandwidth, and some of you don't seem to even cache it, while it's multiple GB big. That is just insane. And meanwhile the githbub plan is still fronting a lot of bandwidth (we bought some a while ago, but it ran out super quick, like under an hour quick), and I am sure they are starting to be done with us, as someone reported to have problems pulling down through LFS. Have a look at this graph: You have it here for free: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@chainsafe/eth2-spec-tests 😄 that's 6000+ spec tests LFS clones over the last 20 days. Each multiple GB of bandwidth (worst case, some may be cached and much, but some may not, and then it gets bad real fast) Please, start using the gzipped tarballs (you can find them on the release page for every release!). It's nicely split up in configuration, separates SSZ-generic and BLS. And is much, much cheaper on bandwidth (it's compressed, and not billed by github) Should we release a torrent with the spec tests? Gzipped tarballs on release page are easier, have a static link, and are not billed. So that would be preferred. Compression also generally helps a lot with the tests, as mainnet tests have lots of redundant info due to state size blow up
